lines.text: Group project. Five names on the cover. So who actually did the work?
lines.headline: Five names. *One worker?*

lines.text: Put one person on a rope, and they pull hard. Add more people, and each one quietly pulls less.
lines.headline: More hands, ==less pull.==

lines.text: In 1979, Bibb Latané, Kipling Williams and Stephen Harkins had students shout and clap as loud as they could, alone or in groups.
lines.say: In 1979, Bibb Lah-tah-nay, Kipling Williams and Stephen Harkins had students shout and clap as loud as they could, alone or in groups.
lines.headline: *Latané, Williams & Harkins,* 1979

lines.text: In pairs, each person made only seventy-one percent of their solo noise.
lines.headline: Noise ==per person.==

lines.text: In groups of six? Just forty percent.
Even blindfolded, when they only believed others were shouting along, they eased off.
lines.headline: Effort *hides in a crowd.*

lines.text: When nobody can tell who did what, effort quietly disappears.
So split the work into named jobs. When each part is visible, everyone pulls.
lines.headline: Make each part ==visible.==

lines.text: Send this to your group chat. You know who it's for.

post.title: Why Group Projects Always Have One Person Doing Everything #shorts
post.description: Social loafing: in 1979 Bibb Latané, Kipling Williams and Stephen Harkins had students shout and clap as loudly as they could, alone or in groups. In pairs each person produced 71% of their solo noise; in groups of six, just 40%. Even blindfolded people who only believed others were shouting with them eased off. Make each person's part visible and identifiable. Latané, B., Williams, K., & Harkins, S. (1979). Many hands make light the work: The causes and consequences of social loafing. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(6), 822-832. #psychology #shorts #socialloafing #groupwork
